title: The physician's prayer
hook: a famous prayer for physicians is attributed to him, though probably written later

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: read with honesty. Keep the brilliance and the blind spot on the same page. Which old line did you hold up to the light? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

A framed page hangs on the wall of a doctor's office. A prayer, in the voice of a physician, asking for love of the work and patience with the sick, and at the bottom, a name: Maimonides. It fits. He was a doctor at court in Cairo. He wrote medical books. Who else would it be? And yet the trail of that prayer leads somewhere else. Yesterday was about reading him honestly. Today's word is a prayer that carries his name, and the question of whose it really is.
screen: `A FRAMED PRAYER.` → `SIGNED: MAIMONIDES.` → `WHOSE IS IT REALLY?`

segments.voice: The physician's prayer. Turn it four ways. First, what it asks. In it a doctor asks God for love of the art and of every creature, for a mind clear at the bedside, and to be kept from greed and the hunger for fame. And it asks that the doctor see in the sick person only a fellow human being in pain. Second, where it comes from. The prayer isn't found in Maimonides' own writings. It appears in print long after his death, in German, and the scholars who have traced it point to a later physician, often named as Marcus Herz. Third, what Maimonides did write about healing. In his commentary on the Mishnah, he treats healing as a duty drawn from the Torah's law of lost property: the command to return what your neighbor has lost, he says, includes helping return a person's lost health. And the Torah itself names God as healer: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." Fourth, attributed, not his. The rabbis cared about who said what. The Talmud teaches that whoever repeats a saying in the name of the one who said it brings redemption to the world. So a careful reader can still love this prayer, can still hang it on the wall, and can still say it, while giving it its true label. A prayer worth keeping, with its true label on it.
screen: `A FELLOW HUMAN BEING IN PAIN.` · `NOT FOUND IN HIS WRITINGS.` · `HEALING AS RETURNING WHAT WAS LOST.` · `SAY IT IN THE NAME OF WHO SAID IT.` · then, large: `ATTRIBUTED, NOT HIS.`

segments.voice: Get still for a moment, and breathe. Bring to mind one healer. A doctor, a nurse, a therapist, a home aide, the person who sat with someone you love. See their hands, their tired face at the end of a shift. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or hold the Torah's words "I am the LORD that healeth thee" for a few breaths. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with gratitude. Then let them go and sit. The bell holds the time.
The physician's prayer. A prayer for doctors credited to Maimonides, which scholars trace to a later hand. Today's word.
Your line: attributed, not his. Today, when you pass on a quote, check whose it really is, and give the credit to the one who said it. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews pray for the sick in synagogue with a blessing called the Mi Sheberach and in the daily Amidah's blessing for healing, and some medical ceremonies read the physician's prayer, often still under Maimonides' name.

original.note: Hebrew: healer, physician; the Torah calls God rofe in Exodus 15:26.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maimonides wrote the physician's prayer.
what it means: it carries his name, but scholars trace it to a later physician; his own teaching on healing lies elsewhere.
what a scholar hears: a German text first printed long after him, often credited to Marcus Herz; Maimonides on Mishnah Nedarim 4:4, reading Deuteronomy 22:2 as a duty to heal.
